title: Unbiased Estimation of Conditional Covariance for Quantum Optomechanics
abstract: Continuous measurements can prepare macroscopic mechanical oscillators in conditional quantum states, but their covariance is difficult to verify. The conventional retrodictive estimator assumes a forward--backward covariance symmetry and can be biased, because physical dynamics such as feedback damping reduces the observability of the state from future records. Here, we derive an exact linear-Gaussian estimator from causal, retrodictive, and smoothed trajectories. For a milligram-scale mirror, it agrees with a Riccati prediction based on parameters fixed independently, while the conventional estimate exhibits a large bias in the covariance-space metric, $d_M \sim 5$. Our method paves the way toward unbiased testing of macroscopic entanglement within a calibrated linear-Gaussian model, which will be applicable to tabletop mirrors as well as gravitational-wave kg-scale test masses.
summary: The paper introduces an unbiased estimator for the conditional covariance of macroscopic mechanical oscillators measured via continuous monitoring. By combining forward, future-likelihood, and smoothed trajectories, it overcomes systematic biases inherent in conventional retrodictive methods. This advancement is crucial for accurately characterizing quantum states, such as entanglement, in tabletop and gravitational-wave scale optomechanical systems.
main_problem: Verifying the conditional covariance of macroscopic mechanical oscillators prepared via continuous measurements is difficult because conventional estimators can be biased due to physical dynamics like feedback damping.
main_result: The proposed three-trajectory estimator provides an exact unbiased estimate for the conditional covariance, showing a significant reduction in bias compared to conventional methods when applied to milligram-scale mirrors.
method: The authors derive and apply an exact linear-Gaussian estimator by augmenting the retrodictive reconstruction with a smoothed trajectory, comparing it against standard two-trajectory estimators.
model_or_system: The system involves macroscopic mechanical oscillators (e.g., milligram-scale mirrors) coupled to optical fields in optomechanics setups, modeled as a linear Gaussian process governed by state-space equations.
key_observables: Conditional Covariance ($V$), Logarithmic Negativity ($	ext{EN}$), and the covariance-space distance metric ($	ext{d}M$).
important_parameters: Milligram-scale mirror mass, gravitational-wave kg-scale test masses, feedback damping rates.
main_assumptions: The method assumes a calibrated linear-Gaussian state-space model; it is not model-free tomography and relies on the structure of the underlying dynamics.
figures_summary: Figure 1 shows the bias ($	ext{d}M$) of conventional estimators vs. detuning/cooperativity. Figure 2 details an experimental record spectrum for a suspended mirror. Figure 3 compares three-trajectory estimates to Riccati predictions, and Figure 4 shows frequency-resolved covariance closure tests.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the difficulty with conventional estimators due to symmetry assumptions, introduces the novel three-trajectory estimator based on smoothing theory, validates it against known Riccati solutions using experimental data from an optomechanical cavity, and concludes by demonstrating its utility for entanglement testing.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses measurement backaction and state estimation in large-scale quantum systems (optomechanics), providing a rigorous tool to test non-classical features like entanglement that are otherwise obscured by measurement noise or flawed estimators.
